title: SpaceX's AI pivot collides with a broader tech selloff, while a rocket failure two states away reshapes the launch queue
description: 🌎 SpaceX's AI pivot collides with a broader tech selloff, while a rocket failure two states away reshapes the launch queue
html:
Market Overview

🌎 SpaceX's AI pivot collides with a broader tech selloff, while a rocket failure two states away reshapes the launch queue

A rough week for growth stocks generally hit the space sector hard, with AI valuation jitters and a broad Nasdaq selloff pressuring most names in this basket. Against that backdrop, SpaceX pushed further into AI infrastructure with a bond sale, a Texas power permit and new orbital compute plans, while a United Launch Alliance failure over the weekend tightened the launch market just as several constellation operators need rides the most. Beyond those stories, a run of contract wins at Redwire and a new defense contract at BlackSky, company specific news was thin this week; several names in this basket traded mostly on macro sentiment rather than their own headlines.


SpaceX (SPCX)
SpaceX shares were volatile all week as the stock traded with the broader AI complex rather than on its own fundamentals. Shares fell 1.26% on Monday, November 16, to $137.36 as the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.49% in a broad tech selloff, with AST SpaceMobile down 12.33% the same session. The stock then jumped 3.16% on Tuesday, November 17, to $141.70 after Bloomberg reported SpaceX could begin selling roughly $4 billion of bonds that week, the first tranche of the $40 billion financing commitment the company disclosed in October to buy Nvidia's next generation Vera Rubin chips; Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management are expected to underwrite the offering, with funds tied to BlackRock and KKR also making financing commitments. The same day, speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, SpaceX chief financial officer Bret Johnsen said the company's first couple of gigawatts of AI compute cost roughly $30 to $35 per watt to build, against an estimated $50 to $60 for the rest of the industry, and that SpaceX plans to expand terrestrial AI compute capacity from just over 2 gigawatts at the end of 2026 to between 5 and 10 gigawatts in 2027. Johnsen also outlined plans to use Starship to launch solar powered orbital compute satellites, targeting an initial demonstration as soon as 2027 and gigawatt scale orbital capacity by 2029. On Wednesday, November 18, the stock added another 1.27% to $143.50; no company announcement was tied to that move, though it came a day after Texas regulators, who had resumed permitting following a pause ordered in September, issued an air permit for SpaceX's planned $24 billion Starbase data center campus, with reported configurations ranging from roughly 35 turbines and 748 megawatts to a larger 1,456-megawatt build-out depending on the source. By Thursday, November 19, shares had given back those gains, falling roughly 3.5% to the $138 range amid a broader market pullback following a weak reception for an unrelated AI IPO. SpaceX's next scheduled lockup event, the final tranche of its 180-day post-IPO restriction, falls on December 8; see this week's Sentiment Signal for a full breakdown of what that means for the stock's tradable float.


AST SpaceMobile (ASTS)
AST SpaceMobile had one of the roughest weeks in the sector, falling as much as 18% to a 52-week low of $27.01 on Tuesday, November 17, before closing at $27.59. Two separate pressures combined to drive the decline. First, a United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after liftoff from Cape Canaveral on Sunday, November 15, destroying 40 satellites bound for Amazon's Leo broadband constellation; while none of AST's own satellites were aboard, the resulting pullback in available launch capacity hit AST particularly hard because the company depends on buying rides from the same small pool of providers, and three of its BlueBird satellites have been sitting at Cape Canaveral since September awaiting a SpaceX launch date. Second, a prospectus supplement around November 17 disclosed that AST had issued 10 million shares of Class A common stock to Firefly Aerospace as part of the cash-and-stock consideration under their rocket engine agreement, with AST receiving no cash for that first tranche of an estimated 10 to 14 million shares, adding modest dilution at an already depressed share price. The stock fell further with the broader market on November 18 and 19, closing around $25 to $26 by midweek. Jim Cramer called the name "a very hard stock to own" on his November 16 broadcast, citing heavy cash burn against a still-unprofitable direct-to-device business.


Redwire (RDW)
Redwire kept adding to its November contract total, announcing on November 19 a roughly $15 million award to supply its Extensible Low-Profile Solar Array, or ELSA, wings to AscendArc for a stackable geosynchronous communications satellite, the company's fourth disclosed contract win of the month and its second commercial ELSA order after an earlier $12.8 million deal with Moog. Redwire said it now has more than 65 solar array wings delivered or in development. Separately, chairman and chief executive Peter Cannito bought 14,144 shares of Redwire stock on the open market on November 16 at $7.07 per share, a modest insider purchase disclosed in a Form 4 filed the following day. Shares still slid with the broader sector for most of the week, from around $7.60 on November 16 to roughly $6.80 by November 18.


Firefly Aerospace (FLY)
Firefly's own news this week was limited to the mechanics of its AST SpaceMobile rocket engine deal: the roughly 10 million AST shares issued to Firefly around November 17 are part of the more than $1.3 billion, three-year agreement the two companies signed on November 6 to supply Miranda and Vira engines for AST's planned heavy-lift Blacklift rocket. The shares are subject to lock-up restrictions and give Firefly a stake in AST's fortunes alongside the cash portion of the deal, even as AST shares fell sharply this week.


BlackSky Technology (BKSY)
BlackSky announced on November 16 a new seven figure Assured contract with what it described only as "a new major international ministry of defense," without naming the country. Under the one year agreement, the customer gets committed, priority tasking of BlackSky's Gen 3 very high resolution imagery and AI enabled analytics over its critical areas of interest, delivered through the company's Spectra platform; BlackSky said the customer moved from initial meetings to a signed Assured subscription in under nine months, with training completed in less than 12 hours after signing. The company framed the deal as evidence of the high margin, recurring revenue model it has been building out internationally. BKSY shares still traded down with the broader sector for most of the week.


Takeaway
This was a week where macro forces, not company news, did most of the driving: a broad AI valuation wobble dragged nearly every name in this basket lower, and a launch failure that touched none of our 13 tickers directly still rippled through the group by tightening an already scarce launch market. SpaceX remains the clearest story in the sector, methodically converting its October AI financing commitment into bonds, power permits and an orbital compute roadmap, while quieter names this week, Rocket Lab, Intuitive Machines, Virgin Galactic, Spire Global, Viasat, MDA Space, Planet Labs and Globalstar among them, had their most recent company news cluster in the days just before this week's window (Rocket Lab's 100th Electron launch and Q3 earnings, Intuitive Machines' Q3 report, Virgin Galactic's Delta-class delay, Planet's Stoke Space launch deal, Globalstar's French spectrum approval) and so traded mostly on the broader tape this week rather than fresh headlines of their own. Watch for confirmation of SpaceX's bond pricing, a firm launch date for AST's delayed BlueBirds, and any read-through from Amazon's and ULA's investigation into the Vulcan failure ahead of Amazon's next attempt, targeted for no earlier than November 23 on an Ariane 6.

🎯THE REAL TEST OF SPACEX'S FLOAT: WHAT DECEMBER 8 ACTUALLY MEANS FOR SPCX

A float that has been expanding by design since June
SpaceX went public in June 2026 holding back the overwhelming majority of its own shares. Only about 4.3% of total shares, the roughly 639 million shares sold in the IPO plus a small overallotment, were freely tradable in the first days after listing. Everything else, insider holdings, employee grants and pre-IPO investor stakes, sat behind a staggered lockup schedule rather than the single cliff-edge expiration that most IPOs use. That structure was deliberate: rather than dumping the whole float on the market at once, SpaceX's bankers built in a sequence of releases timed to specific calendar and earnings events, so the stock's available supply has been expanding in stages for five months rather than all at once.


The stages so far
The first release came on August 6, when roughly 911.5 million shares, about 20% of insider holdings, became eligible for sale, lifting the tradable float from around 4% to roughly 12% of shares outstanding. A second, larger tranche followed two trading days after SpaceX's October 20 third-quarter earnings report: a release of roughly 1.3 billion shares, by several accounts the single largest tranche of the year, pushing cumulative eligible shares to an estimated 4.349 billion. Both events came and went without the sharp selloffs some investors had feared, in part because strong operating results, particularly the October quarter's $14.6 billion in revenue, gave holders a reason to stay put even as more stock became available to sell.


What is actually left for December 8
December 8 is the end of the standard 180-day lockup that covers most remaining restricted holders, the final scheduled release in the sequence that began in August. Multiple outlets tracking the prospectus put the size of this last tranche at up to roughly 797.6 million shares, about 5.9% of the 13.58 billion shares outstanding as of mid-October, worth in the neighborhood of $113 billion at SpaceX's November 17 closing price of $141.70. Separately, other estimates put the resulting increase in SpaceX's tradable float at around 17.6% from its current level, a meaningfully smaller single jump than either of the two prior releases in percentage terms, even though the dollar value is larger given how much the stock has climbed since the IPO. Crucially, this tranche does not touch the shares held by chief executive Elon Musk and a small group of senior executives, representing roughly 40% economic ownership and about 85% of voting control, which remain locked until June 2027.


Why short interest looks tame heading in
If the market were bracing for a rerun of August's volatility, short interest would typically be climbing into the event. Instead, the data point the other way: shares sold short fell roughly 15.7% over the two weeks to October 30, to an estimated 141.1 million shares, which by the same analysis represented only about 3% of SpaceX's then-current tradable float, a sharp decline from the 30%-plus levels seen around the August lockup and the October earnings report. Because short interest is measured as a percentage of a float that itself keeps growing, a falling percentage does not necessarily mean fewer bearish bets in absolute terms, but the combination of declining short share count and a shrinking percentage suggests that, unlike earlier in the year, options and short sellers are not obviously positioning for a repeat shock around this date.


What the academic and sell-side evidence actually says
Patrick Corrigan, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame who studies IPO structures, has noted that lockup expirations produce an average share price decline of around 1.5%, a modest figure that reflects the fact that most lockup expirations do not force actual selling, they merely remove a restriction. Jay Ritter, who directs the IPO research initiative at the University of Florida, adds the important caveat for a stock like SpaceX: a small float magnifies the price impact of any given swing in supply or demand, so even a release that looks modest in percentage terms can move the stock more than the same percentage release would for a more conventionally floated company. That combination, a historically mild average effect, layered onto a stock whose float has been unusually constrained all year, is the central tension investors are weighing into December 8.#


Takeaway
December 8 completes the sequence SpaceX's bankers designed back in June, not a surprise event; at roughly a 17.6% increase to the tradable float, it is smaller in relative terms than either the August or October releases that the stock absorbed without lasting damage, and the muted short interest heading in suggests the market is not bracing for a shock. The bigger swing factor for SPCX between now and year end is probably not the lockup itself but the roughly $4 billion first tranche of SpaceX's $40 billion AI financing plan pricing in the bond market, and whether the terms of that debt sale color how investors read the stock's balance sheet just as more of the float comes free to trade. The next milestone after that is June 2027, when Musk's own shares, and with them the vast majority of SpaceX's remaining supply overhang, come off restriction for the first time.
